e-9227.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070862/assets/54ae1bc6614a1fe70fac039fbdd3defd2aeeceb3648679ee3d4c9ad10f6f15b5.png)

Consider the matrices above. Given that $A = P J P^{-1}$ is a Jordan canonical decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the second column of the matrix $P?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070862/assets/a985e5861e7360654b98ca334fac6d55f435e271dcc52b313e350f74a4c755c5.png)
e-9227.worked_solution:
First, notice that the Jordan matrix $J$ consists of one Jordan block $J = J_2(1).$ 

Therefore, the columns of $P$ form the following chain: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{2}(1) & : & {v}_{2}\overset{A-1I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-1I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

As a result, the second column of $P$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to $\lambda=1.$ 

Now, computing $A-1I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-1I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]-1[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Among the given vectors, only $\mathbf x$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2,$ since

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070862/assets/624e955f479c8193ff32f3bebf0decb7b1d6b45fb5ec44db637d956e3a8d1ea7.png)
and
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070862/assets/0855b40d83950bcdfeda8447e74187f498fbfe73050e1e8fd7755a1ad4b1dbd0.png)

Therefore, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\overset{A-1I\,}{\to }[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\overset{A-1I\,}{\to }0.\end{aligned}
$$

The other vectors do not satisfy this condition.

Consider the matrices above. Given that $A = P J P^{-1}$ is a Jordan canonical decomposition of $A,$ find the value of $\dfrac{a}{b}.$
e-9088.worked_solution:
From the Jordan matrix $J,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$$
\lambda_1=\lambda_2=4.
$$

As a result, the first column of $P$ corresponds to an eigenvector of the eigenvalue $\lambda=4.$ 

Now, computing $A-4I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}]-(4)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 4 \\ -4 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 4 & 0 \\ -4 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain $x_1=-x_2.$ Hence, the general solution is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070862/assets/ca51c47bc0e065fa8ec1303f235f5b5e0c818bf271abbfb90ba96219fd6dd91a.png)

Therefore, setting $x_2=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070862/assets/34e1d2e3dcdfd3c46c3e2ca5360fd596e307efe042f6676413736a100d058155.png)

Finally, $\dfrac{a}{b}=\dfrac{-1}{1} = -1.$

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-6 & -8 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}],\,J=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices above. Given that $A=PJ{P}^{-1}$ is a Jordan canonical decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the second column of the matrix $P?$

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,y=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,z=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that the Jordan matrix $J$ consists of one Jordan block $J={J}_{2}(-2).$  

Therefore, the columns of $P$ form the following chain: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{2}(-2) & : & {v}_{2}\overset{A-(-2)I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-(-2)I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

As a result, the second column of $P$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to $\lambda =-2.$ 

Now, computing $A-(-2)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & -8 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -8 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Among the given vectors, only $x$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2,$ since

$$
(A-(-2)I)x=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -8 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2\end{aligned}]=y,
$$

and, therefore,

$$
(A-(-2)I)^{2}x=(A+2I)y=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -8 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],
$$

and we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\overset{A-(-2)I\,}{\to }[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\overset{A-(-2)I\,}{\to }0.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The other vectors do not satisfy this condition.

content.knowledge_point: Identifying Columns of a Transformation Matrix in a Jordan Decomposition
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-16 & -25 \\ 9 & 14\end{aligned}],\,J=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices above. Given that $A=PJ{P}^{-1}$ is a Jordan canonical decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the first column of the matrix $P?$

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,y=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,z=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -3\end{aligned}]
$$
content.worked_solution:
First, notice that the Jordan matrix $J$ consists of one Jordan block $J={J}_{2}(-1).$ 

Therefore, the columns of $P$ form the following chain: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{2}(-1) & : & {v}_{2}\overset{A-(-1)I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-(-1)I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

As a result, the first column of $P$ is an eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda =-1.$ 

Now, computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}-16 & -25 \\ 9 & 14\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-15 & -25 \\ 9 & 15\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Among the given vectors, only $z$ is an eigenvector of $A,$ since

$$
(A-(-1)I)z=[\begin{aligned}-15 & -25 \\ 9 & 15\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 \\ -3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

and we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\overset{A-(-1)I\,}{\to }0.\end{aligned}
$$

The other vectors do not satisfy this condition.

Consider the matrices above. Given that A=PJP−1 is a Jordan canonical decomposition of A, which of the following could be the second column of the matrix P?

x=[−33],y=[1−2],z=[2−2]

a
x only
b
y only
c
x and z only
d
y and z only
e
z only
Submit

decision.explanation: Let N=A-2I=[[-2,-2],[2,2]]. The second column v must satisfy Nv≠0 and N²v=0. Here Nx=Nz=0, while Ny=(2,-2)=z and Nz=0. Thus only y works. The matrix P=[z,y] has determinant -2, so it is invertible and gives the required decomposition.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}],\,J=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices above. Given that $A=PJ{P}^{-1}$ is a Jordan canonical decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the second column of the matrix $P?$

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,y=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,z=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that the Jordan matrix $J$ consists of one Jordan block $J={J}_{2}(2).$ 

Therefore, the columns of $P$ form the following chain: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{2}(2) & : & {v}_{2}\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

As a result, the second column of $P$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2$ corresponding to $\lambda =2.$ 

Now, computing $A-2I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Among the given vectors, only $y$ is a generalized eigenvector of rank $2,$ since

$$
(A-2I)y=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]=z,
$$

and, therefore,

$$
(A-2I)^{2}y=(A-2I)z=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],
$$

and we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }0.\end{aligned}
$$

The other vectors do not satisfy this condition.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}],\,J=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}a & ∗ \\ b & ∗\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices above. Given that $A=PJ{P}^{-1}$ is a Jordan canonical decomposition of $A,$ find the value of $\frac{b}{a}.$
after.worked_solution:
From the Jordan matrix $J,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=2.
$$

As a result, the first column of $P$ corresponds to an eigenvector of the eigenvalue $\lambda =2.$ 

Now, computing $A-2I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]-(2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{1}{1}=1.$

content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}],\,J=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}a & ∗ \\ b & ∗\end{aligned}]

Consider the matrices above. Given that $A=PJ{P}^{-1}$ is a Jordan canonical decomposition of $A,$ find the value of $\frac{b}{a}.$
content.worked_solution:
From the Jordan matrix $J,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=2.
$$

As a result, the first column of $P$ corresponds to an eigenvector of the eigenvalue $\lambda =2.$ 

Now, computing $A-2I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]-(2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].

content.knowledge_point: Finding Elements of a Jordan Canonical Decomposition for a 2x2 Matrix: The First Column Case
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}9 & 4 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}],\,J=[\begin{aligned}7 & 1 \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}a & ∗ \\ b & ∗\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices above. Given that $A=PJ{P}^{-1}$ is a Jordan canonical decomposition of $A,$ find the value of $\frac{b}{a}.$
content.worked_solution:
From the Jordan matrix $J,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=7.
$$

As a result, the first column of $P$ corresponds to an eigenvector of the eigenvalue $\lambda =7.$ 

Now, computing $A-7I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-7I & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 4 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}]-(7)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ -1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{1}{-2}=-\frac{1}{2}.$

content.knowledge_point: Finding Elements of a Jordan Canonical Decomposition for a 2x2 Matrix: The First Column Case
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}11 & -8 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}],\,J=[\begin{aligned}7 & 1 \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}a & ∗ \\ b & ∗\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices above. Given that $A=PJ{P}^{-1}$ is a Jordan canonical decomposition of $A,$ find the value of $\frac{b}{a}.$
content.worked_solution:
From the Jordan matrix $J,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=7.
$$

As a result, the first column of $P$ corresponds to an eigenvector of the eigenvalue $\lambda =7.$ 

Now, computing $A-7I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-7I & =[\begin{aligned}11 & -8 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]-(7)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -8 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -8 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{1}{2}.$

content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}],\,J=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & a \\ 1 & b\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices above. Given that $A=PJ{P}^{-1}$ is a Jordan canonical decomposition of $A,$ find the value of $2a+2b.$
content.worked_solution:
From the Jordan matrix $J,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=2.
$$

As a result, we obtain that 

- the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ of the eigenvalue $\lambda =2,$

- the second column of $P$ corresponds to the vector ${v}_{2}$ such that $(A-2I){v}_{2}={v}_{1}.$

Now, computing $A-2I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}]-(2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -2 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, the matrix equation $(A-2I){v}_{2}={v}_{1}$ is equivalent to the system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & -1 \\ -2 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}-{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get  

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2} \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $2a+2b=2\cdot (-\frac{3}{2})+2\cdot 1=-1.$
